name: Chocolate Brown
lede: Chocolate Brown is a dark, grayish reddish brown named for the food, and also the color that red lead pigment turns when it decays.

sections.title: A food name
sections.body:
Paterson defines chocolate brown as a dark brown, and records it as a food additive that gives chocolate cake mixes their brown color, also called Brown HT [1]. The shorter color Chocolate is a separate entry, one of the X11 set with the hex code D2691E, which is a much lighter orange-brown than this swatch [1]. The name appears in the ISCC-NBS system of 1955, in block 61 (dark grayish reddish brown, about 3.3 units from the swatch), and in RAL 1927 [2].

Neighbors are [[coffee]], [[cocoa]], [[umber]] and [[bistre]] [2].

sections.title: When red lead turns chocolate brown
sections.body:
Chocolate brown is also what some pigments become. Red lead darkens to a chocolate brown on wall paintings in China, Turkestan and Afghanistan, and that darkening has been recorded in Indian miniatures, Japanese paintings and Swiss wall paintings [3][4]. Gettens describes the change as strongest when red lead is exposed to light, while outdoors it may turn pink or white through the formation of lead sulphate [4].

So a chocolate-brown area in an old painting may once have been a lively orange-red [3][4]. Copper chromates show a similar range, with one compound varying from yellow to copper-red to chocolate-brown [5].

sections.title: Brown as the color of earth and cloth
sections.body:
In Derek Jarman's *Chroma*, brown is the color of corduroy worn by the ploughman and the rich man with acres, and of a chocolate-brown blanket kept from childhood [6]. The book treats brown with nostalgia, not chemistry, and the swatch here is the shade a corduroy or blanket suggests [6][2].

Humic acids in soil are chocolate brown too, which links the name to earth as much as to cocoa [7].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color near this swatch appears in 1,889 works, or 7.9 per cent, more common than 93 per cent of the named colors [8]. Its rate is highest in the 1500s and again in the 1900s, at 7.9 per cent of paintings from the latter [8]. It works as a shadow color: about 78 per cent of its coverage sits in the darkest part of a painting's lightness order [9]. Whistler's portrait of George W. Vanderbilt has it covering 95 per cent of the canvas [9].

These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so some of these browns were originally other colors, as the red lead cases show [8][3].
